stem: Why is aluminium used to make aircraft?

options.content: It has a low density.
options.rationale: A light metal (strong when alloyed) keeps the aircraft's mass low.

options.content: It is a good conductor of electricity.
options.rationale: Conductivity is not what an aircraft body needs.

options.content: It is magnetic.
options.rationale: Aluminium is not magnetic, and magnetism is not needed.

options.content: It has a high density.
options.rationale: A dense metal would make the aircraft heavy.

explanation: Aircraft must be as light as possible, so a low-density metal is used. Aluminium alloys are light and strong.

stem: Which properties make copper suitable for electrical wiring?

options.content: hardness and strong magnetism
options.rationale: Copper is not magnetic, and hardness is not needed for wires.

options.content: low density and a high melting point
options.rationale: Low density is not a property of copper (it is quite dense).

options.content: resistance to corrosion, and nothing else
options.rationale: Corrosion resistance helps, but the key properties are conductivity and ductility.

options.content: very good electrical conductivity and ductility
options.rationale: It carries current well and can be drawn into thin wires.

explanation: Copper is an excellent conductor of electricity and is ductile, so it can be drawn into wires.

stem: True or false: aluminium is used to make food containers because it resists corrosion.

answerSpec.feedbackTrue: Correct: a thin layer of aluminium oxide protects the metal from air, water and food.
answerSpec.feedbackFalse: It is true: aluminium's oxide layer stops it corroding, so it is used for cans, foil and trays.

explanation: Aluminium resists corrosion because a thin, tough oxide layer covers its surface. This makes it suitable for food containers.

stem: Why is aluminium used for **overhead power cables**?

options.content: It has a low density and is a good conductor of electricity.
options.rationale: Light cables put less strain on the pylons.

options.content: It has a high density, so the cables hang straight.
options.rationale: A high density would make the cables heavier.

options.content: It is the best conductor of electricity of all metals.
options.rationale: Silver and copper conduct better; aluminium is chosen for its combination of conductivity and low density.

options.content: It is a poor conductor, so the cables do not get hot.
options.rationale: A cable must conduct electricity well.

explanation: Overhead cables must conduct electricity and be light enough to hang between pylons. Aluminium has a good electrical conductivity and a low density.

stem: Match each use with the property that makes the metal suitable.

right.content: low density and good electrical conductivity

explanation: Aircraft: low density. Overhead cables: low density and good conductivity. Food containers: resistance to corrosion. Electrical wiring: conductivity and ductility. High density is not wanted for any of these uses.

stem: Platinum-group metals mined on the Great Dyke are used mainly in which product?

options.content: drinks cans and food tins
options.rationale: Drinks cans are made of aluminium or steel.

options.content: overhead power cables strung between pylons
options.rationale: Cables are made of aluminium (with a steel core).

options.content: catalytic converters in vehicle exhausts
options.rationale: They catalyse the conversion of harmful exhaust gases.

options.content: corrugated roofing sheets
options.rationale: Roofing sheets are made of galvanised steel or aluminium.

explanation: Platinum, palladium and rhodium are excellent catalysts that do not corrode, so they are used in catalytic converters to reduce harmful exhaust gases.

stem: Which metal is used in rechargeable batteries for mobile phones and electric vehicles?

options.content: lithium
options.rationale: Lithium-ion batteries are light and give a high voltage.

options.content: platinum
options.rationale: Platinum is used mainly in catalytic converters.

options.content: gold
options.rationale: Gold is used in electrical connectors and jewellery, not as the battery material.

options.content: chromium
options.rationale: Chromium is used in stainless steel and plating.

explanation: Lithium is the least dense metal and is very reactive, so lithium-ion cells are light and give a high voltage.

stem: Why is gold used for jewellery?

options.content: It is unreactive, so it stays shiny, and it is easy to shape.
options.rationale: It does not tarnish or corrode.

options.content: It has a low density, so the jewellery is light.
options.rationale: Gold is one of the densest metals.

options.content: It is cheap and easy to find in Zimbabwe.
options.rationale: Gold is rare and expensive.

options.content: It is very reactive, so it forms attractive coloured compounds.
options.rationale: Gold is one of the least reactive metals.

explanation: Gold is lustrous and very unreactive: it does not tarnish in air or water. It is also very malleable, so it can be worked into fine shapes.
hints: Think about what happens to the surface of most metals over time.

stem: Why are chromium and nickel added to iron to make cutlery and kitchen sinks?

options.content: They make the iron softer so it can be bent by hand.
options.rationale: Stainless steel is hard.

options.content: They lower the density of the iron so it floats.
options.rationale: Chromium and nickel do not make steel float.

options.content: They produce stainless steel, which resists rusting.
options.rationale: Stainless steel stays shiny in contact with water and food.

options.content: They make the iron magnetic.
options.rationale: Magnetism is not the reason for adding them.

explanation: Chromium and nickel alloyed with iron form stainless steel, which resists corrosion, so it is used for cutlery, sinks and surgical instruments.
hints: What problem do iron objects have in a wet kitchen?

stem: Name the metal with the lowest density of all metals, used in rechargeable batteries.

rejected.feedback: Sodium is light, but lithium has the lowest density of all metals.
Lead is very dense; it is used in car batteries, not lightweight rechargeable cells.

explanation: Lithium has the lowest density of all metals. Lithium-ion batteries are used in phones, laptops and electric vehicles.

stem:
An electricity company is choosing a metal for new overhead cables.

| Metal | Density / g/cm³ | Relative electrical conductivity | Strength | Resistance to corrosion |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| aluminium | 2.7 | 63 | low | good |
| copper | 8.9 | 100 | medium | good |
| iron | 7.9 | 17 | high (as steel) | poor (rusts) |

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Which metal is the best electrical conductor?

options.content: aluminium
options.rationale: Aluminium conducts well, but less well than copper.

options.content: copper
options.rationale: Copper has the highest relative conductivity in the table.

options.content: iron
options.rationale: Iron has the lowest conductivity.

options.content: they all conduct equally well
options.rationale: The relative conductivities are very different.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Suggest why aluminium is chosen instead of copper.

options.content: It is stronger than copper.
options.rationale: The table shows aluminium is weaker.

options.content: It conducts electricity better than copper.
options.rationale: The table shows copper conducts better.

options.content: It is much less dense, so the cables are lighter.
options.rationale: Lighter cables need fewer, less sturdy pylons.

options.content: It corrodes faster than copper.
options.rationale: Corroding faster would be a disadvantage, and both resist corrosion well.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Aluminium cables are usually wound around a core of steel. Use the table to suggest why.

points.description: Steel is strong, so the core supports the weight of the cable (aluminium alone is not strong enough)

parts.explanation: Aluminium has a low strength. The steel core is strong, so it carries the weight of the long span of cable while the aluminium carries the current.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Why is copper, not aluminium, used for the wiring inside a house?

options.content: Copper rusts less than aluminium does in walls.
options.rationale: Neither rusts; rusting is the corrosion of iron.

options.content: Copper is less dense than aluminium, so it is lighter.
options.rationale: Copper is denser.

options.content: Aluminium does not conduct electricity well in indoor conditions.
options.rationale: Aluminium conducts anywhere; copper is simply the better choice for house wiring.

options.content: Weight hardly matters indoors, and copper conducts better and is ductile.
options.rationale: Over short lengths, copper's higher conductivity matters more than its density.

explanation: Copper is the best conductor, but its high density makes long overhead cables too heavy, so aluminium (low density, good conductor) is used, with a strong steel core for support. Inside buildings weight is unimportant, so copper's better conductivity and ductility make it the choice.
hints: Which property in the table matters most for a cable hanging between pylons?

stem: A 1.00 km length of overhead cable has a cross-sectional area of 1.00 cm². (Density of aluminium = 2.70 g/cm³; density of copper = 8.96 g/cm³; 1 km = 100 000 cm)

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the mass, in kg, of the cable if it is made of aluminium.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate the mass, in kg, of the same cable made of copper.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Use your answers to explain one advantage of aluminium for overhead cables.

points.description: The aluminium cable is about 3.3 times lighter (626 kg less per km), so pylons can be lighter / further apart

parts.explanation: The aluminium cable has about one third of the mass of the copper cable (270 kg compared with 896 kg per kilometre), so the pylons have less weight to support.

explanation: Mass $=$ density $\times$ volume. Volume $= 1.00\ \text{cm}^2 \times 100\,000\ \text{cm} = 100\,000\ \text{cm}^3$. Aluminium: $270\ \text{kg}$; copper: $896\ \text{kg}$. Aluminium cables are about 3.3 times lighter.
workedSolution:
1. (a) $V = 100\,000\ \text{cm}^3$; $m = 100\,000 \times 2.70 = 270\,000\ \text{g} = 270\ \text{kg}$.
2. (b) $m = 100\,000 \times 8.96 = 896\,000\ \text{g} = 896\ \text{kg}$.
3. (c) The aluminium cable is much lighter for the same size.
hints: Convert grams to kilograms by dividing by 1000.

stem: Copper is used for hot-water pipes in some buildings. Which pair of properties makes it suitable?

options.content: It is a poor conductor of heat, so the water inside the pipes stays hot.
options.rationale: Copper is a very good conductor of heat.

options.content: It reacts with water to form a protective oxide.
options.rationale: Copper does not react with water.

options.content: It has a low density and is magnetic.
options.rationale: Copper is dense and not magnetic.

options.content: It does not react with water, and it can easily be bent into shape.
options.rationale: Copper resists corrosion and is malleable.

explanation: Copper does not react with water and resists corrosion, and it is malleable enough to bend and join. (It is a good conductor of heat, which is why hot pipes are often lagged.)
hints: What must a water pipe never do?

stem: Zimbabwe mines gold and platinum. Explain why gold is used for the electrical connectors in mobile phones, and why platinum is used in catalytic converters. [4]

points.description: Gold is a good conductor of electricity
Gold is very unreactive / does not corrode or tarnish, so connections stay reliable
Platinum is a good catalyst (speeds up the conversion of harmful exhaust gases)
Platinum is unreactive / has a high melting point, so it is not damaged or used up in hot exhaust gases

answerSpec.modelAnswer: Gold conducts electricity well and it is very unreactive, so it does not corrode or tarnish; a thin gold layer keeps the connectors working reliably for years. Platinum is an excellent catalyst for the reactions that change carbon monoxide, oxides of nitrogen and unburnt fuel into less harmful gases. Because platinum is unreactive and has a high melting point, it is not damaged or used up by the hot exhaust gases.

explanation: Each use depends on matching properties: gold = conductor + unreactive; platinum = catalyst + unreactive and heat-resistant.
hints: Give one property and its link to the use for each metal.

stem: Complete the sentences.

payload.template: Aluminium is used for aircraft because of its low {{blank:a}}. Copper is used for electrical wiring because it is a very good conductor and it is {{blank:b}}. Aluminium is used for food containers because it resists {{blank:c}}.

explanation: Aluminium: low density (aircraft) and corrosion resistance (food containers). Copper: good conductor and ductile (wiring).

stem: Aluminium is widely used for cooking pots. Which set of properties makes it suitable?

options.content: poor conductor of heat, high density and very reactive with water
options.rationale: A pot must conduct heat well.

options.content: good conductor of heat, low density and resistant to corrosion
options.rationale: Heat passes quickly to the food, the pot is light, and it does not corrode.

options.content: magnetic, brittle and soluble in water
options.rationale: Aluminium is none of these.

options.content: low melting point, so it melts evenly
options.rationale: A cooking pot must not melt.

explanation: Aluminium conducts heat well, is light to lift and resists corrosion thanks to its oxide layer.
hints: What does a cooking pot need to do?

stem: Silver conducts electricity slightly better than copper. Why is copper, not silver, used for the wiring in houses?

options.content: Silver is not ductile.
options.rationale: Silver is very ductile.

options.content: Silver is far more expensive, and copper conducts almost as well.
options.rationale: Cost is decisive when large amounts of wire are needed.

options.content: Silver does not conduct electricity when cold.
options.rationale: Silver conducts at all normal temperatures.

options.content: Copper has a lower density than silver, which matters inside walls.
options.rationale: Weight is not important for wiring inside walls; cost is the reason.

explanation: Choosing a material is not only about the best property. Copper's conductivity is almost as high as silver's, and copper costs a small fraction of the price.

stem: Steel rods are placed inside concrete columns and beams in buildings. Which property of steel is most important for this use?

options.content: low density
options.rationale: Steel is quite dense; strength is what matters.

options.content: lustre
options.rationale: The rods are hidden in the concrete.

options.content: high strength
options.rationale: Steel strengthens the concrete and stops it cracking under load.

options.content: high electrical conductivity
options.rationale: Electricity does not flow through building beams.

explanation: Steel is strong and cheap, so it is used to reinforce concrete in buildings and bridges.
hints: What job does the rod do inside the concrete?

stem: State **one** use of nickel.

rejected.feedback: Nickel is not mainly used for jewellery; it is used in stainless steel and batteries.

explanation: Nickel is used mainly in stainless steel (with chromium and iron), and also in rechargeable batteries, plating, coins and as a catalyst (for example, for adding hydrogen to vegetable oils to make margarine).

stem: True or false: gold is used in electronic devices because it conducts electricity and does not corrode.

answerSpec.feedbackTrue: Correct: gold contacts stay clean and conducting for many years.
answerSpec.feedbackFalse: It is true: gold is a good conductor and is very unreactive, so it does not corrode.

explanation: Gold is used for connectors and contacts in phones and computers because it conducts well and never corrodes.

stem: Aluminium is a reactive metal, high in the reactivity series, yet it is used for drinks cans and cooking foil. Why does it not corrode away?

options.content: The drinks and foods it holds are always neutral.
options.rationale: Many drinks and foods are acidic; the oxide layer is the reason.

options.content: A thin, tough oxide layer stops air and water reaching the metal.
options.rationale: The oxide layer protects the metal underneath.

options.content: Aluminium is below hydrogen in the reactivity series.
options.rationale: Aluminium is well above hydrogen.

options.content: Aluminium does not react with oxygen in the air.
options.rationale: It reacts readily with oxygen; that is how the protective oxide layer forms.

explanation: As soon as aluminium is exposed to air it forms a thin, unreactive layer of aluminium oxide that sticks firmly to the metal and protects it from further corrosion.
hints: What forms on the surface of aluminium in air?
